author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A federal judge has split the difference in New Hampshire’s fight over student identification cards and voting: the state may keep its new law removing student IDs from the list of photo IDs that must be accepted at the polls, but election officials may not be told to ignore those cards entirely when deciding whether a voter’s identity can be verified.

U.S. District Judge Joseph Laplante issued the preliminary order on Oct. 2 in a lawsuit brought by the Coalition for Open Democracy. The [court’s written order](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/new-hampshire/nhdce/1:2026cv00647/68549/63/) denied the organization’s request to block House Bill 323 for the November general election. That means the law’s central change remains in place for the Nov. 3 election: a student ID is no longer an expressly valid form of photo identification for obtaining a ballot.

The ruling also limits how that change can be administered. New Hampshire law directs a voter without one of the listed photo IDs to a supervisor of the checklist, who must review the voter’s qualifications and determine whether the person’s identity can be verified. The statute contains a catch-all standard allowing other evidence that reasonably establishes it is more likely than not that the person is who they claim to be. Laplante said the Secretary of State’s April directive went beyond the law when it told voters and election workers that student IDs could not be used for identity purposes at all.

The judge therefore preliminarily enjoined the state from enforcing the directive to the extent it prohibits or discourages officials from reviewing student identification cards as evidence under those verification procedures. The order tells Secretary of State David Scanlan’s office to issue revised guidance for the November election as soon as practicable. The guidance must explain that student IDs are not restored to the list of expressly valid IDs, but may be considered together with other available evidence when officials decide whether a voter’s identity is established.

That distinction is important for students who arrive at a polling place without a driver’s license, passport, military ID or state-issued non-driver identification. A student card alone does not automatically entitle someone to a ballot under the new law. It can, however, be part of the evidence presented to the supervisor of the checklist, along with whatever other information the voter can provide. The court’s order leaves the final verification decision with local election officials rather than guaranteeing a particular outcome for every card.

The policy was adopted through HB 323, which the New Hampshire General Court describes as a bill requiring a government-issued photographic means of identification in order to vote. The [legislative record](https://gc.nh.gov/bill_Status/billinfo.aspx?id=413&version-id=3853) shows that Gov. Kelly Ayotte signed the measure on April 3 and that it took effect June 2. Before then, qualifying student cards from New Hampshire schools and certain other institutions were among the forms of identification expressly accepted under the state’s voter-ID law, provided they showed the voter’s name and photograph and were within the required issuance or expiration period.

Scanlan’s office had translated the new law into broad public instructions before the court ruled. The [Secretary of State’s election guidance](https://www.sos.nh.gov/election-day-voting) says student IDs cannot be used to prove identity and directs voters without an acceptable ID to seek a voucher from a town or city clerk or the Secretary of State for use at the Department of Motor Vehicles. The court did not invalidate that stand-alone-ID rule; it required the state to clarify the separate safety-valve process for voters who lack a listed ID.

New Hampshire Public Radio, reporting for the Keene Sentinel, described the order as a rejection of the Secretary of State’s categorical approach while noting that the law itself remains in effect for the general election. The [Boston Globe](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/06/metro/student-ids-voting-new-hampshire-court-decision/) likewise reported that election workers may still consider student IDs as backup proof of identity under the court’s reading of state law. Both accounts emphasize that the practical details now depend on the revised instructions sent to town and city election officials.

The case remains a live legal dispute rather than a final ruling on the constitutionality of HB 323. Laplante’s order addressed preliminary relief before the November election and found that the plaintiff had not shown enough at this stage to block the statute itself, while finding a likely constitutional problem with the state directive’s categorical exclusion of student IDs. For students and election workers, the immediate question is narrower: whether local officials receive and follow the promised guidance in time for Nov. 3, and how the catch-all evidence standard is applied when a voter has no other qualifying photo ID.
dek: A federal judge left New Hampshire’s student-ID restriction in place for Nov. 3 but ordered the state to let election officials consider those cards as evidence when verifying voters without another qualifying ID.
headline: Federal judge narrows New Hampshire student-ID voting restriction
sourceName: U.S. District Court for the District of New Hampshire
